subtype: Approach: watching a friend who rides well and copying [Action]
passage: I'm Naveen, and from my window I could see Shalini on the pavement every evening. She did not jump on the cycle like the rest of us. She sat on the wall and watched her neighbour Rekha ride: the way Rekha put one foot on the pedal, pushed off with the other, and kept her eyes level. Then Shalini copied it, one step at a time, whispering the order. She wobbled and stopped. "Rekha didi, what did I do wrong?" Rekha laughed and showed her how to keep her knees loose. By Friday, Shalini pedalled the whole length of the pavement, and Rekha clapped.

qa.q: What did Shalini whisper while copying Rekha?
qa.a: Shalini whispered the order of the steps.

qa.q: What might Shalini feel when asking Rekha what she did wrong?
qa.a: Shalini seems eager and humble, since asking for correction shows she wants to improve and trusts Rekha.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Shalini use if watching is not enough, and why?
qa.a: Shalini could ask Rekha to hold the seat for the first tries or practise gliding without pedals. That gives balance practice with a helper close by.

qa.q: How does Naveen see Shalini's way of learning?
qa.a: Naveen watches from the window over several evenings, so Naveen probably sees patient, careful practice that is different from everyone else's jumping straight on.

grounding: A girl watches how her neighbour starts, pushes off and keeps eyes ahead, copies the steps one by one and asks for correction, as seen by an observer.

subtype: Approach: setting small goals such as ten metres, then twenty [Revision]
passage: Nilesh could ride only a few metres before his legs stopped and his feet dropped. Every day the same. "I'm not getting anywhere," he told Rajni, kicking the tyre. "Maybe you are," said Rajni. "You never measured." That evening Nilesh took chalk and drew a line at ten metres, another at twenty. Tomorrow he reached the first line on his second try. The day after, he passed it easily and fell just before the second line. He rubbed his knee, but he was grinning, because he could now see that each attempt took him further than the last.

qa.q: What did Nilesh draw on the ground?
qa.a: Nilesh drew a line at ten metres and another at twenty.

qa.q: What did Nilesh feel when he told Rajni he was not getting anywhere?
qa.a: Nilesh felt stuck and discouraged, which is why he kicked the tyre.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Nilesh try, and why?
qa.a: Nilesh could ask an older rider to watch and point out one thing to fix. A fresh pair of eyes can spot problems that are hard to feel.

qa.q: How does Rajni's remark change how Nilesh sees his progress?
qa.a: Rajni said Nilesh had never measured, so the chalk lines let Nilesh see improvement and the grin at the end shows that it worked.

grounding: Feeling stuck at a few metres, a boy chalks ten- and twenty-metre marks so counting improvement shows him he is getting better despite falls.

subtype: Approach: repeating the list aloud again and again [Action]
passage:
Kiran: Neem sticks, two paint tubes, a clay lump, cotton wool, glitter glue, a sponge, string!
Indrajit: Are you talking to yourself?
Kiran: Craft class tomorrow. Seven things. Neem sticks, two paint tubes...
Indrajit: Race you to the gate!
Kiran: Not now, bhaiya! Neem sticks, two paint tubes, clay lump, cotton... cotton...
Indrajit: Look, a butterfly!
Kiran: Oh, Indrajit! Now where was I? Cotton wool, glitter glue... what else?
Indrajit: How should I know?
Kiran stood at the door, counting on her fingers. She had only five.

qa.q: How many items did Kiran have to bring?
qa.a: Kiran had to bring seven items.

qa.q: What did Kiran feel when she could name only five items?
qa.a: Kiran felt annoyed and worried, since Indrajit's interruptions made two items slip away. 😰

qa.q: What alternative approach could Kiran use, and why?
qa.a: Kiran could write the seven items down when she hears them, or picture each one in a place at home. A written or pictured list stays even if someone interrupts.

qa.q: How does Indrajit see Kiran's chanting?
qa.a: Indrajit sees a sister talking to herself and joins in with a race and a butterfly, so Indrajit sees a game and does not realise it matters to Kiran.

grounding: A girl repeats seven craft items aloud all the way home, but the chanting works only for a while and two items are lost when her brother interrupts.

subtype: Approach: making a funny sentence from the first letters [Thinking]
passage: In the school library, Gautam stared at the list: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The exam was tomorrow. He tried saying them again and again. The teacher, Vidya, looked up from her desk. "What would help you?" Gautam frowned, then his eyes lit up. "The first letters! M, V, E, M, J, S, U, N. Let me make a sentence. My Very Elegant Monkey Jumps Skipping Under Nets." He laughed. "A monkey with a skipping rope! Now I can see it." He wrote it in the corner of his notebook and repeated it once, then closed his eyes and recited the planets in order without a mistake.

qa.q: What silly sentence did Gautam make?
qa.a: Gautam made the sentence 'My Very Elegant Monkey Jumps Skipping Under Nets.'

qa.q: What did Gautam think the sentence would do for his memory?
qa.a: Gautam thought the funny picture of a monkey with a skipping rope would connect the planets so he could see and recall them in order.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Gautam use for the planets, and why?
qa.a: Gautam could draw the planets in a row or say them in rhythm as a chant. A picture or a rhythm gives another route to the order.

qa.q: How might Vidya see Gautam's idea?
qa.a: Vidya asked a simple question and let Gautam find the answer, so Vidya probably feels pleased to see the boy solve the problem alone.

grounding: A boy makes a silly sentence from the first letters of the planets, and the story links the separate items so they are recalled in order.

subtype: Approach: linking each item to a place in the house [Thinking]
passage: On the way home from the village school, Usha listened to her teacher's list in her head: glue bottle, scissors, chart paper. At home, Nazia was waiting in the yard. "How will you remember three things till tomorrow?" Usha closed her eyes. "I'm walking through our house. The glue bottle is stuck on the front door, so I can't get in. The scissors are on the sofa, snipping the cushion. And the chart paper is on the fridge, flapping like a flag." She opened her eyes. "Door, sofa, fridge." Nazia laughed. The next morning Usha packed all three at once without a single pause.

qa.q: Where did Usha picture the glue bottle?
qa.a: Usha pictured the glue bottle on the front door.

qa.q: Why did Usha imagine the items in odd places?
qa.a: Usha found the silly pictures easier to remember, and felt confident that walking through the house in her mind would bring each item back. 😊

qa.q: What alternative approach could Usha use, and why?
qa.a: Usha could write the three items on her hand or a slip of paper, or ask a parent to remind her. A written note works even on a tired day.

qa.q: How does Nazia see Usha's method?
qa.a: Nazia asked how three things could be remembered and laughed at the pictures, so Nazia finds it funny and clever, and may want to try it.

grounding: A child imagines a glue bottle on the door, scissors on the sofa and chart paper on the fridge, and walking through the house in her mind brings each item back.

subtype: Approach: writing it down as soon as it is told [Action]
passage: Damini, look at this small diary I still keep. I'm Pankaj, and when I was ten, my teacher, Mr Kulkarni, called out what we needed for the next day's science class: a torch, a spoon, a small mirror and a piece of black paper. Most children nodded and hoped to remember. I took out my little diary and wrote the four items at once, in a hurry, before the next lesson began. That night I checked it twice, once at dinner and once before sleep. In class, I was the only one with all four things. Writing had made my head free to think about the experiment.

qa.q: What four items did the teacher ask for?
qa.a: The teacher asked for a torch, a spoon, a small mirror and a piece of black paper.

qa.q: Why did the narrator write the items at once?
qa.a: Pankaj wanted the list safe in the diary instead of in a head that might forget, and felt sure this would help.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped the narrator have all four items, and why?
qa.a: Writing them down at once and checking twice helped, because the list stayed correct and the narrator could check it later.

qa.q: How did the other children in the class fare?
qa.a: Most children only nodded and hoped to remember, and Pankaj was the only one with all four things, so the others probably missed some items.

grounding: Pankaj writes down the items the teacher names in a small diary at once, which frees the mind from holding them and lets the list be checked later.

subtype: Approach: trusting memory and not writing it [Pitfall]
passage: Note from Manasi's mother, Sudha. Manasi came home from school saying the teacher had given four things for the trip: water bottle, cap, snack box, an old towel. "I'll remember," she said, refusing my offer of pen and paper. By evening she stood in the kitchen with a small frown. "Bottle, cap, snack box, and... it's gone." She rang a classmate, but the phone rang out, and nobody answered. She sat by the window twisting her hair. In the morning she packed what she had and went to school without the towel, looking unsure. I hope she will keep a note next time.

qa.q: How many things did Manasi recall by evening?
qa.a: Manasi recalled three things.

qa.q: What was Manasi feeling when nobody answered the phone?
qa.a: Manasi was worried and uneasy, shown by sitting at the window twisting her hair and setting off without the towel. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Manasi use next time, and why?
qa.a: Manasi could write the list when the teacher says it or ask a classmate for a copy. A written list does not fade by evening.

qa.q: How does Sudha see the situation?
qa.a: Sudha had offered pen and paper and was refused, so Sudha probably feels concerned and hopeful that Manasi will accept a note next time.

grounding: A girl trusts her memory instead of writing four trip items, recalls only three by evening and cannot reach a classmate to check.

passage: The little grocery shop near the bus stand would shut at eight, and the clock said twenty to. Bidisha's mother had given her a long list in a hurry: apples, bananas, spinach, tomatoes, onions, milk, curd, paneer. Her brother Ojas hopped beside her. "That's so many!" Bidisha stopped outside the door. "Three groups," she said. "Fruits first: apples, bananas. Vegetables: spinach, tomatoes, onions. Then milk, curd, paneer." She repeated it in the queue, and went through the shop one shelf at a time. Nothing was missed, and Ojas carried the bag home, proud to be useful.

qa.q: When would the grocery shop shut?
qa.a: The shop would shut at eight.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling outside the shop, and how did the grouping help?
qa.a: Bidisha felt pressed for time and a little overwhelmed by the long list, but three groups turned one big list into three small ones she could hold.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Bidisha use, and why?
qa.a: Bidisha could ask her mother to write the list down or take a picture of the list to check in the shop. That would keep the items in front of her even when rushed.

qa.q: How does the shopping trip look to Ojas?
qa.a: Ojas hopped along, said there were so many items and later carried the bag proudly, so Ojas felt part of the job and pleased to help.

grounding: A child sorts a long shopping list into fruits, vegetables and dairy before entering the shop, so three small groups replace one long list.

subtype: Approach: drawing tiny pictures next to each item [Action]
passage: Vishal hated writing lists. Words on paper felt like homework. But tomorrow was art day, and he needed to pack a ruler, a pencil and a bottle of water. On a small card he drew a tiny yellow pencil, a long ruler with stripes and a blue bottle with a cap. He propped the card against the mirror. The next morning, his little sister Avni came in while he was getting dressed. "What's that?" "My list. Look, what do you see?" "Pencil, ruler, water!" Vishal grinned. He packed all three, and later drew her a card for her own bag.

qa.q: What did Vishal draw on the card?
qa.a: Vishal drew a pencil, a ruler and a bottle.

qa.q: How does Vishal feel about writing lists, and what does he do about it?
qa.a: Vishal dislikes writing because it feels like homework, so he draws pictures that he enjoys and can understand at a glance.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Vishal use if he loses the card, and why?
qa.a: Vishal could keep the items always in the same spot in the bag or check them against a list at the door. A fixed place needs no reading.

qa.q: How does Avni experience Vishal's picture list?
qa.a: Avni read the pictures at once and later got a card of her own, so Avni finds it easy to understand and probably enjoys having a list too.

grounding: A boy who dislikes writing draws a small pencil, ruler and bottle on a card, and the pictures help him and his younger sister remember what to pack.

subtype: Approach: testing himself by covering the list [Revision]
passage: I'm Sharmila. I read my list of ten things for the science kit before bed, then checked against it and found I had forgotten two. That felt bad. So I covered the list with my copybook and tried to say every item aloud. I got seven. I peeked and tried again. Nine. Again. This time I said all ten, even the boring ones: the ruler and the plastic cups. Francis, my cousin, was listening from the sofa and clapped when I was done. Then I put the list away, went to sleep, and in the morning I could still say them all before breakfast.

qa.q: How many items did Sharmila get right on the first try with the list covered?
qa.a: Sharmila got seven items.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel on finding two items missing, and what did Sharmila decide?
qa.a: Sharmila felt bad about the missing two, so Sharmila decided to cover the list and test until all ten could be said.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Sharmila use, and why?
qa.a: Sharmila could put a tick beside each item when packing, or link items to places in the house. Another method helps if memory alone slips.

qa.q: How might Francis have seen Sharmila's practice?
qa.a: Francis listened from the sofa and clapped, so Francis was probably impressed and supportive, seeing a cousin who kept trying until it was right.

grounding: After finding two items missing, Sharmila covers the list and tries to say all items again until they are right, then sleeps on it.
